content.title: About
content.content: Venison is a lean meat from deer, rich in protein and low in fat. In this preparation it is simmered in a flavorful tomato‑based sauce with onion, carrot, celery and herbs, resulting in a juicy and aromatic dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison is considered a more diet‑friendly meat compared with beef because of its low saturated‑fat content.
Traditionally, venison has been a staple in the cuisines of northern regions where deer are abundant.
Tomato sauce adds lycopene, an antioxidant that enhances the health profile of the dish.
Deer meat contains higher levels of iron than most other meats.
In some cultures venison is served on special occasions as a symbol of abundance.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Venison provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The low amount of saturated fat makes it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Rich in iron and zinc
items.content: Iron supports oxygen transport, while zinc aids immune function.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Vitamins B12 and B6 help maintain nervous system health and metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: The tomato sauce contributes lycopene, an antioxidant that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to game meat.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Venison is rich in purines, which can be problematic for people prone to gout.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Game can harbor parasites; it should be cooked to a safe internal temperature.

items.title: Sodium in the sauce
items.content: Tomato sauces often contain added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve venison with tomato sauce alongside whole‑grain sides, mashed potatoes, or couscous. The dish pairs well with red wine or berry‑based sauces. Leftovers reheat nicely on low heat with a splash of water or broth.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.
